prompt:
`main.o` calls `sqrt`. Using traditional GNU ld archive processing, this link fails with an undefined reference to `sqrt`, but swapping the order fixes it. Why?

```
gcc -static -lm main.o -o app
```

options.text: `-lm` must always come last because of a GCC parsing rule about flags
options.explanation: It isn't a parsing rule about flags. The reason is how the linker scans archives.

options.text: `sqrt` is a compiler built-in, so it doesn't need linking at all
options.explanation: Compilers sometimes inline `sqrt`, but here the error shows a real call remained. The question is why the library didn't satisfy it.

options.text: Static linking can't use the maths library
options.explanation: `libm.a` exists for exactly this purpose. Static linking works fine with the right order.

options.text: The linker scans archives once, in order, pulling in only members that resolve symbols already undefined; when it saw `libm.a`, nothing needed `sqrt` yet
options.explanation: Correct. By the time `main.o` introduced the undefined `sqrt`, `libm.a` had already been passed over.

workedExample: When GNU ld first considers libm.a, main.o has not introduced its sqrt reference. Later it reads main.o, but does not automatically revisit that earlier archive. Placing main.o before -lm fixes this dependency order. Archive groups can request rescanning, and LLD’s handling differs. The initial undefined-symbol set need not be empty: startup objects may already contribute references.
